title: Words that changed sides
text: Live long enough and every language drifts, and English drifts {{1}}. Nice once meant foolish, from Latin nescius, ignorant; silly meant blessed; awful meant {{2}} of awe; and a girl was a child of either sex. None of these was a {{3}} — meaning change is normal, unstoppable and mostly invisible while it happens. Linguists {{4}} the drifts: broadening, as holiday swelled from holy day to any day off; narrowing, as deer shrank from animal in general to the specific {{5}}; and the strange reversals, where a word {{6}} its own pole — egregious travelled from outstanding to outstandingly bad. The changes {{7}} the young first, which is why every generation hears its grandchildren corrupting the language, and why every generation is wrong: Chaucer was complained about too. The lesson is {{8}} for anyone who loves words — the dictionary is not a law code but a photograph, taken of a language that was already moving while the shutter was open.

gaps.explanation: 'English drifts constantly' — never stops; conservatively = cautiously or in the traditional way.
'awful meant full of awe' — only 'full of' completes the sense; fell is the past of fall and foul means disgusting.
'none of these was a mistake' — an error to be corrected; misgiving = a feeling of doubt.
'linguists classify the drifts' — arrange them into categories; clarify = make clear.
'deer shrank to the specific species' — the biological category; the sound-alike 'spices' are kitchen ingredients.
'a word crosses its own pole' — moves from one end to the other; cradle = hold gently.
'the changes catch the young first' — take hold of them; patch = mend.
'the lesson is humbling' — it deflates our confidence; bumble = move clumsily, fumble = handle clumsily.
